rationale: Evidence from iteration 6 (score 588.8, best so far): the oval finishes 20/20 (1.89 s, 0.8 line-loss events, rms 0.007). The s-bend finishes 14/20 (progress 0.93), up from 4/20 when the array was 5 sensors at +/-0.06 m. The slalom is still 0/20, with progress 0.16, 0.75 line-loss events per run, and every run ending off_track. Widening the array to 7 sensors at +/-0.08 m fixed most of the s-bend failures but did not move the slalom, so lateral reach of the array is no longer the main limit there. Earlier results suggest the slalom fails at its first fast direction change: the robot loses the tape and then leaves the 0.06 m off-track limit. Two hypotheses are tested together. H1: at base_speed 1.0 the robot cannot turn fast enough through the slalom's back-to-back bends, so it loses the tape. Reducing speed to 0.9 gives it more time to correct. H2: yaw inertia is too high for quick direction changes. Inertia scales with (body_length^2 + body_width^2), so shortening the body from 0.18 to 0.14 m reduces it by about 15 percent, and mass drops from 0.8 to 0.7 kg, which also lowers inertia while keeping the drivetrain the same. Sensors, weights, kp 6.5, kd 2.0, ki 0.2 and line_loss are unchanged, so the effect of the change is isolated to speed and inertia. Expected result: slalom progress rising above 0.3 with fewer line losses; the oval still finishes at about 2.0 to 2.1 s, which costs about 1 to 2 points on the time term. Risks: slower base speed lowers the oval time term, and a shorter body may make the robot less stable on straights (watch steering_oscillation). If the slalom still loses the line on its first swing, the next step is kp 7.0 with kd 2.2 (stronger correction). If the oval oscillates above 0.4, the next step is kd 1.7.
